title: The Judiciary
tagline: Supreme Court, High Courts, subordinate courts and Lok Adalats: jurisdiction, independence and the writs.

overview.intro: The judiciary is the branch that interprets the Constitution and protects the citizen against the State, and the syllabus builds it upwards from the Supreme Court to the district court. This chapter takes the Supreme Court’s composition and appointment, its independence from the other organs and its four jurisdictions, then the High Courts with their wider writ power, the distinction between a District Judge and a Sessions Court, and finally the Lok Adalats that settle disputes before they reach a court at all. The two habits worth building are to name the jurisdiction and then its article, and to explain how a court remains independent without sounding as though it is unaccountable.

learningOutcomes: State the composition, qualifications, appointment and retirement ages of the Supreme Court and the High Courts.
Classify the Supreme Court’s original, appellate, advisory and revisory jurisdictions with articles.
Explain how the judiciary is independent of the executive and the legislature, quoting the relevant safeguards.
Describe the High Court’s writ jurisdiction and judicial review, and distinguish Article 32 from Article 226.
Distinguish a District Judge from a Sessions Court and state the advantages of a Lok Adalat.

learn.title: The Supreme Court: composition, appointment and jurisdiction

blocks.text: The Supreme Court consists of the Chief Justice of India and such other judges as Parliament may authorise, at present a sanctioned strength of the Chief Justice plus 33 judges. Judges are appointed by the President after consultation with such of the judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts as the President thinks fit — a consultation that the collegium system, developed through the judges’ cases, has converted into the primacy of the judiciary’s own recommendation. To be appointed, a person must be a citizen of India, must have been a judge of a High Court for at least five years, or an advocate of a High Court for at least ten years, or be a distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President. A Supreme Court judge retires at 65 and may be removed only by a procedure akin to impeachment. The Court’s jurisdiction runs in four channels: original jurisdiction in disputes between the Union and the States or between States, and in the enforcement of fundamental rights; appellate jurisdiction over civil, criminal and constitutional matters and from the High Courts; advisory jurisdiction on any question of law or fact referred by the President under Article 143; and revisory jurisdiction, including its power to recall and rehear a case under Article 137.

items: Article 124 fixes the composition and appointment; Article 123 in the ordinance power, Article 143 in the advisory power and Article 137 in the power of review.
Qualifications: citizen of India; five years as a High Court judge, or ten years as a High Court advocate, or a distinguished jurist.
Retirement at 65 years; removal only by impeachment-like procedure, so security of tenure protects independence.
Original jurisdiction under Article 131 extends to disputes between the Union and a State and between two States.
Appellate jurisdiction under Article 133 and 134 covers civil, criminal and constitutional appeals, and Article 136 is the special leave power.
Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India, and Article 144 binds all authorities to act in aid of the Supreme Court.

blocks.caption: Four jurisdictions of the Supreme Court
rows: Union-State and inter-State disputes, and fundamental rights enforcement
Civil, criminal, constitutional appeals and special leave
Reference by the President on a question of law or fact
Review or recall of its own judgment

items.note: A State sues the Union over the diversion of river waters, and the suit is filed directly in the Supreme Court because only that Court can hear a Union-State dispute.
A party asks the Supreme Court to grant leave to appeal against a High Court judgment on the ground of a substantial question of law, invoking Article 136.

blocks.text: Judicial independence is not a slogan but a set of specific mechanisms, and a good answer lists them as mechanisms. Security of tenure: a judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court can be removed only by the difficult impeachment procedure, never at the pleasure of the executive, and the settlement of salaries and allowances by Parliament after each financial year means the legislature cannot use pay as pressure. The bar of post-retirement practice stops the executive from offering lucrative work to a judge who knows judgment day is coming, and the power of contempt lets the Court protect its own proceedings. The doctrine of judicial review, protected as part of the basic structure of the Constitution, means the Court may strike down a law that violates the Constitution, and the power to issue writs gives the citizen a direct remedy. Finally, the appointment process itself, in which the collegium recommends and the President acts, keeps the executive from choosing judges who will agree with it. Together these provisions explain why an Indian court can hold the State to account without becoming an unelected government.

items: Security of tenure: removal only by impeachment, and pleasure of the President cannot be used to remove a judge.
Salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and settled by Parliament, so they cannot be used as leverage.
Bar of practice after retirement prevents post-retirement inducements from influencing judgments.
Power to punish for its own contempt, under Articles 129 and 215, protects the Court’s authority.
Judicial review of legislation and of executive action, held to be part of the basic structure of the Constitution.
Collegium system of appointment: the Chief Justice and senior judges recommend, and the executive formalises the appointment.

items.note: The Supreme Court invalidates a statute that abridges a fundamental right, using judicial review so that the legislature’s will does not become the final word on the Constitution.
A person who publishes material calculated to obstruct the course of justice is punished for contempt, which is how the Court protects its own proceedings.

items.meaning: The power of the courts to examine whether a law or executive action conforms to the Constitution and to strike it down if it does not.
The core features of the Constitution that even a constitutional amendment cannot destroy, judicial review among them.
Protection of a judge from removal except by the prescribed impeachment procedure.
The body of senior Supreme Court judges whose recommendation has primacy in judicial appointments.

learn.title: The High Courts: composition, jurisdiction and writs

blocks.text: Every State has a High Court, and one High Court may serve two or more States by order of the President. A judge must be a citizen of India and must either have held judicial office for ten years, or been an advocate of a High Court for ten years, or be a distinguished jurist; the Chief Justice is appointed by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice of India and the Governor of the State, and other judges are appointed by a collegium of the Chief Justice of India and the judges of the Supreme Court and the High Court concerned. Judges retire at 62. The High Court has original jurisdiction in respect of fundamental rights and, where a State has conferred it, in other matters; appellate jurisdiction in civil, criminal and constitutional cases; revisory jurisdiction over its own subordinate courts; and the power of judicial review. Article 226 gives it the power to issue directions, orders and writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights and for any other purpose, which is wider than Article 32, and Article 215 declares every High Court a Court of Record with power to punish for contempt of itself.

items: Composition: a Chief Justice and such other judges as the President may determine; retirement at 62 years.
Qualifications: ten years of judicial office, or ten years as an advocate of a High Court, or a distinguished jurist.
Original jurisdiction over fundamental rights; appellate jurisdiction in civil, criminal and constitutional matters; revisory jurisdiction over subordinate courts.
Article 226 writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto, for fundamental rights and for any other purpose.
Article 215 declares the High Court a Court of Record with powers to punish for its own contempt.
Judicial review extends to the State legislature and the State executive, just as it extends to Parliament at the Union level.

blocks.caption: The five writs

Commands a public authority to perform a legal duty
Authority refusing a hearing it owes
Stops a lower court from proceeding beyond jurisdiction

Setting aside an illegal administrative order
Asks by what authority an office is held

A court declines mandamus where the duty claimed is discretionary, because mandamus issues only for a legal duty that is complete and enforceable.

learn.title: Subordinate courts and the Lok Adalats

blocks.text: At the base of the judicial system are the civil and criminal courts of a district, and the syllabus asks for one precise distinction. The District Judge is the senior civil judge of a district, appointed by the Governor of the State in consultation with the High Court, who tries the most important civil cases and supervises the civil courts of the district; when the same officer tries criminal cases in the district he or she sits as a Sessions Judge and tries serious criminal cases, with the power to impose any sentence including death subject to confirmation by the High Court. Appeals run from the subordinate courts to the District Judge and then to the High Court, and every court in the district is under the superintendence of the High Court under Article 227. Beside this hierarchy sits the Lok Adalat, a conciliation forum constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, which takes up pending cases, pre-litigation disputes and compoundable matters, charges no court fee, and whose award is signed by the parties and is binding on them like a decree of a civil court with no appeal against it.

items: District Judge: appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court; hears important civil cases and superintends the district’s civil courts.
Sessions Judge: the same officer trying criminal cases in the sessions division, empowered to award any sentence including death, which needs High Court confirmation.
Criminal cases lie below the sessions level with magistrates, and appeals pass to the Sessions Judge and then to the High Court.
High Court superintendence of all subordinate courts in the State comes from Article 227.
Lok Adalat: no court fee, and once the matter is taken up any fee already paid in court is refunded.
Lok Adalat award: signed by the parties, binding like a decree, and no appeal lies against it.

items.note: A Sessions Judge convicts an accused of a grave offence and sentences the accused to imprisonment, and because the sentence is death it must be confirmed by the High Court before it is carried out.
A motor accident claim is settled for a lump sum before trial; the parties sign the award, the court fee is refunded and no appeal lies from that award.

items.meaning: The senior civil judge of a district who hears important civil cases and supervises the civil courts of the district.
The criminal court presided over by a Sessions Judge trying serious criminal cases in the sessions division.
A court whose proceedings are recorded for perpetual memory and which may punish for its own contempt, under Articles 129 and 215.
A conciliation forum under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 whose award is binding like a decree.

blocks.text: The judiciary section rewards precision and punishes length without structure. For a question on the Supreme Court, give composition, qualifications, appointment, tenure and jurisdiction in that order, since the marking scheme follows it. For a question on independence, do not write in general terms about the judges being above politics: list the mechanisms — security of tenure, salary protection, the bar on post-retirement practice, contempt power, judicial review and the collegium — and attach one article to at least three of them. For a writ question, state for each writ the order it issues, the authority it is served on and a one-line instance, which is exactly the three-part structure the mark scheme wants. Finally, keep the High Court and the Supreme Court answers parallel: a candidate who writes two entirely different structures for the two courts usually misplaces a jurisdiction in one of them.

items: Order the Supreme Court answer as composition, qualifications, appointment, tenure, jurisdiction.
For independence, name the mechanism and attach an article; general statements score little.
For each writ, give the order, the authority served and a one-line instance.
Keep High Court and Supreme Court answers parallel so that jurisdictions do not get transposed.

items.note: One paragraph per writ: what the court orders, against whom, and when it issues — habeas corpus for detention, mandamus for a refused duty, certiorari to quash, prohibition to stay, quo warranto for an office.

items.text: A short note on Lok Adalat
items.note: Constituting authority, the matters it takes up, no court fee, award signed by parties, award binding like a decree and no appeal.

keyPoints: The Supreme Court is the Chief Justice of India plus such other judges as Parliament authorises; judges retire at 65.
Qualification: five years as a High Court judge, or ten years as a High Court advocate, or a distinguished jurist.
The Supreme Court has original, appellate, advisory and revisory jurisdictions, the advisory one being Article 143.
Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts in India.
Judicial review, security of tenure, salary protection, the bar on post-retirement practice and the contempt power secure independence.
A High Court judge must have ten years of judicial office or practice and retires at 62.
Article 226 gives the High Court wider writ power than Article 32 because it covers any purpose, not only fundamental rights.
The five writs are habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto.
Articles 129 and 215 make the Supreme Court and every High Court Courts of Record with power to punish for their own contempt.
The District Judge hears important civil cases; sitting as a Sessions Judge the same officer tries criminal cases.
A death sentence awarded by a Sessions Judge requires confirmation by the High Court.
A Lok Adalat charges no court fee and its award is binding like a decree with no appeal against it.
examFocus: Jurisdiction questions want the article attached: 131, 133-136, 143 and 137 for the Supreme Court; 226 and 227 for the High Court.
Independence answers must list mechanisms rather than assert that judges are impartial.
Writ questions are marked in three parts for each writ: the order, the authority served and the instance.
The District Judge against Sessions Court distinction is a two-line answer: same officer, civil against criminal work.

vocabulary.meaning: The authority of a court to hear and decide a particular class of case.
A formal order issued by a court under Articles 32 and 226 directing an act or restraint.
A writ requiring a detained person to be produced before the court so that the legality of the detention can be examined.
A writ commanding a public authority to perform a legal duty it has refused.
A writ by which a higher court quashes an order made by a lower court or tribunal beyond its jurisdiction.
The power to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution and strike down what fails.
A court whose records are evidence of what was said and which may punish contempt of itself.
The decision signed by the parties at a Lok Adalat, which operates as a decree of a civil court.

questions.prompt: A judge of the Supreme Court of India retires at the age of:
questions.explanation: Article 124 fixes the retirement age of a Supreme Court judge at 65 years, against 62 for a High Court judge.

questions.prompt: The writ issued to produce a detained person before the court is:
questions.explanation: Habeas corpus commands the authority to produce the body of the detained person so the detention can be tested.

questions.prompt: Which article gives the High Court the power to issue writs for any purpose and not only for fundamental rights?
questions.explanation: Article 226 is wider than Article 32 because it covers the enforcement of fundamental rights and any other purpose.

questions.prompt: The award of a Lok Adalat is:
options: Binding on the parties like a decree, with no appeal
Enforceable only with the consent of the court
questions.answer: Binding on the parties like a decree, with no appeal
questions.explanation: Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 the award is signed by the parties and is binding as a decree, and no appeal lies from it.

questions.prompt: The Supreme Court of India is a court of __________ and may punish contempt of itself.
questions.explanation: Articles 129 and 215 declare the Supreme Court and every High Court to be Courts of Record.

questions.prompt: A __________ judge tries the important civil cases of a district and supervises the other civil courts of the district.
questions.explanation: The District Judge is the senior civil judge of the district, appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court.

questions.answer: Article 32 is the power of the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of the fundamental rights, and it is itself a fundamental right so it cannot be suspended except as permitted during an emergency. Article 226 empowers the High Court to issue writs, directions and orders for fundamental rights and for any other purpose, so it is wider in scope; its exercise is subject to the rules of the High Court and to the doctrine that the Supreme Court’s exercise of Article 32 ordinarily prevails.
questions.explanation: The difference lies in the scope: fundamental rights only for Article 32, and fundamental rights plus any other purpose for Article 226.

questions.prompt: State three safeguards that ensure the independence of the judiciary.
questions.answer: First, security of tenure: a judge can be removed only by the difficult impeachment procedure, not at the pleasure of the executive. Second, salaries and allowances are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India and settled after each financial year, so the legislature cannot use them as pressure. Third, a judge may not practise before any court in India after retirement, which removes the incentive to please the government before leaving office. The power to punish for contempt and the doctrine of judicial review add to these safeguards.
questions.explanation: Security of tenure, financial protection and the bar on post-retirement practice are the three mechanisms that carry the marks.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a District Judge and a Sessions Judge?
questions.answer: They are usually the same officer. As District Judge the officer hears the more important civil cases of the district and supervises the civil courts of the district; when the same officer tries criminal cases in the sessions division, the officer sits as a Sessions Judge, may award any sentence including death, and a death sentence must be confirmed by the High Court.
questions.explanation: The distinction is the subject matter: civil work and supervision as District Judge, criminal trials as Sessions Judge.

questions.prompt: Describe the composition and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India.
questions.answer: The Supreme Court consists of the Chief Justice of India and such other judges as Parliament may from time to time authorise, the sanctioned strength being the Chief Justice and 33 other judges. Judges are appointed by the President after consultation with such judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts as the President thinks fit, and in practice the collegium’s recommendation has primacy; a candidate must be a citizen of India with five years’ service as a High Court judge, or ten years as a High Court advocate, or be a distinguished jurist. Retirement is at 65 and removal follows the impeachment-like procedure. Jurisdiction runs in four channels: original jurisdiction in Union-State and inter-State disputes and in fundamental rights under Article 131; appellate jurisdiction in civil, criminal and constitutional matters and by special leave under Articles 133 to 136; advisory jurisdiction on any question of law or fact referred by the President under Article 143; and revisory jurisdiction including review of its own judgments under Article 137, with the law it declares binding on all courts under Article 141.
questions.explanation: Composition, qualifications, appointment, tenure and the four jurisdictions each with their articles.

questions.prompt: Explain the powers and jurisdiction of a High Court and describe the five writs it may issue.
questions.answer: A High Court has original jurisdiction in proceedings for the enforcement of fundamental rights and in other matters the State may confer, appellate jurisdiction in civil, criminal and constitutional cases, revisory jurisdiction over its own subordinate courts, and the power of judicial review over State legislation and executive action. Under Article 226 it may issue directions, orders and writs for fundamental rights and for any other purpose, and Article 215 declares it a Court of Record with power to punish for its own contempt; under Article 227 it superintends all courts and tribunals in the State. The five writs are habeas corpus, which requires a detained person to be produced so the legality of detention can be examined; mandamus, which commands a public authority to perform a legal duty; prohibition, which stops a lower court or tribunal from proceeding beyond its jurisdiction; certiorari, which quashes an order already made beyond jurisdiction; and quo warranto, which requires a person to show by what authority an office is held.
questions.explanation: Jurisdiction heads with articles, then each writ with the order it issues and the situation it answers.

questions.prompt: A public servant holds an office for which the prescribed qualification is a university degree, and the servant does not possess one. Analyse which writ may be issued and why the other writs do not fit.
questions.answer: Quo warranto is the appropriate writ: it calls upon the holder of a public office to show by what authority the office is held, and where the person does not possess the qualification prescribed for the office the holding is unauthorised and the court may declare the office vacant. Habeas corpus does not fit because there is no detention of the person. Mandamus does not fit because the servant is not refusing to perform a legal duty owed to the complainant; the defect is in the holding of the office rather than in a failure to act. Prohibition does not fit because it restrains a court or tribunal from proceeding, and no such proceeding is afoot. Certiorari does not fit for the same reason, since it quashes an order already made by a subordinate authority in excess of jurisdiction, whereas here the complaint is about the qualification for the office itself rather than about a particular order.
questions.explanation: Quo warranto targets the authority to hold office; the other three writs address detention, refused duties and proceedings, none of which is present.
